clinicalPearls: Instability spans a spectrum from subluxation to frank dislocation and is broadly categorised by direction (anterior, posterior, multidirectional) and by aetiology (traumatic structural versus atraumatic).
Anterior instability is by far the most common and typically follows a traumatic anterior dislocation with the arm in abduction and external rotation.
Younger age at first traumatic dislocation is the strongest predictor of recurrence, reflecting soft-tissue healing capacity and activity demands.
A Bankart lesion (anteroinferior labral detachment) and a Hill-Sachs impaction defect of the posterolateral humeral head are the classic structural correlates of anterior instability.
Quantify glenoid and humeral bone loss carefully; engaging bipolar lesions and significant glenoid deficiency predict failure of soft-tissue-only repair.
Posterior instability is easily missed and should be suspected after seizures, electrocution or a posteriorly directed force on a flexed adducted arm.
Atraumatic multidirectional instability is associated with generalised ligamentous laxity and responds primarily to a prolonged programme of rotator cuff and scapular rehabilitation.
The apprehension and relocation tests support anterior instability, while a positive jerk or Kim test suggests posteroinferior pathology.
reference.pathophysiology: Glenohumeral stability depends on the balance between static restraints (the labrum, glenohumeral ligaments and capsule, concavity-compression and negative intra-articular pressure) and dynamic restraints (the rotator cuff, long head of biceps and coordinated scapular motion). Traumatic instability usually results from a discrete injury that detaches the anteroinferior labrum and capsule from the glenoid rim (Bankart lesion), sometimes with an associated bony fragment or an impaction fracture of the humeral head, compromising the static checkrein. Repeated episodes cause progressive capsulolabral attenuation and escalating bone loss, lowering the threshold for further events. Atraumatic and multidirectional instability instead reflect a capacious redundant capsule and constitutional collagen laxity, sometimes compounded by neuromuscular incoordination and voluntary positioning, so that the humeral head translates excessively without a single structural lesion.
additionalDifferentials: Rotator cuff tear, particularly in older patients after dislocation
Brachial plexus or axillary nerve injury following dislocation
Scapular dyskinesis contributing to functional instability
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs including axillary and specialised views to confirm reduction and detect bony lesions
CT with three-dimensional reconstruction to quantify glenoid and humeral head bone loss
MR arthrography to delineate labral, capsular and ligamentous injury
Examination under anaesthesia to grade translation and directionality
Neurological assessment of axillary nerve and brachial plexus function after dislocation
redFlags: Neurovascular deficit after dislocation, especially axillary nerve palsy or vascular compromise
Inability to reduce a dislocation or a locked posterior dislocation
First-time dislocation in an older patient, which carries a high risk of concomitant rotator cuff tear
Recurrent instability with progressive bone loss threatening the success of soft-tissue repair
reference.prognosis: Traumatic anterior instability in young, active individuals has a high recurrence rate with non-operative treatment, whereas anatomical stabilisation restores stability in most, provided bone loss is addressed. Atraumatic multidirectional instability generally responds well to committed rehabilitation, though outcomes are poorer when a voluntary or behavioural component persists.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise a posterior dislocation, which is commonly missed on inadequate radiographic views.
Underestimating glenoid or humeral bone loss and performing a soft-tissue repair destined to fail.
Attempting surgical stabilisation in behavioural or voluntary instability without adequate rehabilitation.
Overlooking an associated rotator cuff tear or nerve injury after dislocation in older patients.
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Trauma
